src: Ordering, counters, and the two meal phrases everyone says.
This one, please (point at the menu)
To call a waiter you say:
저기요 = excuse me (there). 야 is rude to staff.
Native 둘 → 두 before the counter 개 (things).
먹었 = past (I ate well). 먹겠 = future (I will eat well).
To call a server over, you say:
저기요 = 'excuse me', to get someone's attention.
Before you start eating, you say:
먹겠습니다 = 'I will eat (well)'; 먹었습니다 is past, for after the meal.
Noun + native number + 개 for things; 둘 → 두.
Glasses take 잔, with the native number 세 in front of it.
계산 = paying the bill; 해 주세요 = please do it.
하나 → 한 before the counter 잔.
맵지 않게 = not spicy; 해 주세요 = please make it.
I ate well (said after the meal)
After the meal is past: 잘 먹었습니다.
하다 → 해 before 주세요: 계산해 주세요.
Noun + 주세요 is the all-purpose order.
Three gimbap, please (write the number in Hangul)
셋 shortens to 세 before 개.
One coffee, please (write the number in Hangul)
Counting cups is native (한 잔), not Sino 일.
Asking where, understanding the answer, taxis and subway.
In a taxi, 'please go to Myeongdong' =
T-money works on subway, bus and most taxis.
In a taxi: 'Please go to Myeongdong' =
여기서 = here; 세워 주세요 = please stop.
다음 = next, 역 = station. 이번 역 = this stop.
Toward a direction → (으)로; 왼쪽 ends in a consonant, so 으로.
Destination → 으로 (after a consonant) or 에, never 에서.
Please go to the airport (to a taxi driver)
Destination takes 으로 or 에. 에서 is where an action happens.
씨, 님, 오빠/언니 — what to call people and when a bare name is rude.
(to older guy, from a girl) What are you doing?
Your coworker Minsu, same age. Safe way to address him:
Name + 씨 is the polite default with peers.
You're a guy; she's two years older. You call her:
Name + 씨 is the polite default for peers and coworkers.
A woman calling her older male friend 민수:
Women say 오빠 to older guys; men say 형.
A man calling his older female friend 지은:
Men say 누나 to older women; women say 언니.
Calling your close friend 지은 by name:
지은 ends in a consonant → 아.
The title opens (or closes) the request.
Minsu, are you free? (to a coworker)
Name + 씨 for a coworker; it opens (or closes) the question.
(a girl to an older guy) What are you doing?
A girl calls an older guy 오빠.
Minsu! What are you doing? (close friend)
민수 ends in a vowel → 야.
지은 ends in a consonant → 아.
To your close friend 민수: 'Minsu, what are you doing?' (casual)
Vowel-final name + 야, casual 뭐 해.
To your coworker 지은: 'Jieun, are you free?' (polite)
Coworkers get name + 씨, and 요 stays on.
Teachers are 선생님, never a name or 씨.
Suggest, invite, agree: ㄹ까요 / ㄹ래요 / 자, and 같이.
What shall we do this weekend?
Sure, what time shall we meet?
See you at 7 at Hongik Univ. station exit 2
Sorry, I have plans that day
Koreans usually confirm a meetup spot with:
Asking what they want: 'Do you want to go together?' =
-자 goes straight onto the stem: 먹 + 자.
Saying yes to an invite with enthusiasm:
좋아요 = sounds good; the others turn it down.
What shall we do this weekend?
몇 시에 = at what time; 보다 doubles as 'meet'.
Shall we go to a café?
Do you want to watch a movie?
What shall we do this weekend?
Let's hang out together! (to a friend)
-자 attaches straight to the stem: 놀 + 자.
Do you want to eat together? (polite, use -(으)ㄹ래요)
To a friend: 'Let's meet at the café' (use -자)
Meeting happens at a place → 에서; 만나 + 자.
ㅋㅋ, ㅠㅠ, dropped particles, and the shorthand everyone uses on KakaoTalk.
Hungry ㅠㅠ what should I eat
ㅋ = the k in 크크 laughter.
Texting your older coworker, you should:
Shorthand is for friends; politeness stays with seniors.
ㅋ is a laugh sound; more ㅋ = funnier.
ㅇㅇ is short for 응 (yeah). ㄴㄴ = no.
With seniors, keep it polite; 넵 is the friendly work 'yes'.
Between friends, drop everything optional: 지금 어디?
ㅠㅠ: the vowels look like tears.
Casual 나, no particle: 나 다 왔어.
Friends drop 요; 뭐 먹지 = what should I eat.
Where are you now? (to a friend)
어디 = where; texts drop the rest.
Text a friend: 'What are you up to?'
Text a friend: 'I'm on my way'
Politeness still exists: 넵 or 네, never ㅇㅇ, with seniors.
You can't say 'two coffees' without one. The ten counters that cover daily life.
둘 → 두 before a counter; drinks take 잔.
분 is the honorific people counter; 명 is neutral.
Where does the number + counter go?
after the noun: 맥주 두 병
before the noun: 두 병 맥주
People take 명, with native 세.
Tickets are flat things → 장; noun + number + counter.
Animals take 마리, with native 세.
스물 shortens to 스무 before a counter.
I drank two bottles of beer
Noun + number + counter, and the particle goes after the counter.
Native 둘 shortens to 두 before a counter.
Two tickets, please (write the number in Hangul)
I have three cats (write the number in Hangul)
I studied for two hours (write the number in Hangul)
Duration is native + 시간 (두 시간). 두 시 alone means 2 o'clock.
And, but, so. Three endings that turn two short sentences into one natural one.
(I) want to go, but I have no time
I'm busy, so I'm not going
I was hungry, so I ate
(I) go to a café and study (there)
I was busy, so I didn't go
'I was busy, so I didn't go' =
'I was busy, so I didn't go' =
Reason + 서; no past before 서.
'(I) go to a café and study (there)' =
가서 links two steps of one trip.
I'm busy, so I'm not going
I was hungry, so I ate
I'm busy, so I'm not going
26 · Telling a story in the past
String past-tense sentences together with 먼저 · 그리고 · 그다음에 · 그래서 · 마지막으로.
First we went to a café
After that we watched a movie
But the movie was too long
What did you do last weekend?
I had lunch a while ago
Time words set the scene first.
그래서 = so; arriving home is 집에, in the past: 왔어요.
그런데 = but; a describing verb takes 이/가; past 길었어요.
Time words usually come first; the past tense always comes last.
After that, we watched a movie
Connector first; a movie is what you watch → 를.
First we went to a café
어제 needs the past: 만나 + 았어요 → 만났어요.
What did you do last weekend?
I had lunch a while ago
Time word first, then past tense.
Resting happens at home → 집에서; 쉬 + 었어요.
But I didn't drink coffee (use 안)
안 goes right before the verb, even in the past.
27 · Describing nouns: 좋은 날씨, 큰 가방
Put an adjective in front of a noun: a big bag, good weather, spicy food.
Vowel stem + ㄴ, in front of the noun.
큰 + noun; the particle goes on the noun.
Cheaper than, more, less, the best. Everything you need to compare and choose.
The bus is cheaper than a taxi
The bus is cheaper than a taxi (same meaning)
Do you have a bigger bag?
'The bus is cheaper than a taxi' =
보다 goes on the thing you compare against.
'The bus is cheaper than a taxi' =
The bus is cheaper than a taxi (start with the bus)
The bus is cheaper than a taxi
The bus is cheaper than a taxi
못 vs 안, -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 / 없어요, and 몰라요 vs 모르겠어요.
I don't eat spicy food (by choice)
I can't eat spicy food (it's too much)
I can't swim (no skill: 못해요, one word)
못 = can't; 안 = choose not to.
Consonant stem + 을 수 있어요 = can.
Asked something you're unsure about, the soft answer is:
모르겠어요 is the softer 'I'm not sure'.
못 = can't, placed right before the verb. 안 = don't (by choice).
Vowel stem 하 + ㄹ 수 있어요.
'I can't exercise' — where does 못 go?
With 하다 verbs, 못 goes between the noun and 해요.
You're asked something and you're not sure. The soft, common reply:
모르겠어요 = I'm not sure; 몰라요 is a flat 'I don't know'.
Vowel stem 가 + ㄹ 수 없어요.
못 right before the verb = can't.
할 수 있어요 = can do; 한국어 하다 = speak Korean.
'Don't know' is its own verb, 몰라요; never 안 알아요.
I can speak Korean a little (use -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요)
하 + ㄹ 수 있어요 = can do.
I don't eat meat (by choice, use 안)
A choice → 안. 못 would mean you can't.
Say what you must do, ask if you have to, and say when you don't.
Do I have to go now?
What do I have to do?
안 … 도 돼요 = it's okay not to.
Only 해요 goes into the past.
-(으)시- and the special verbs: 드시다, 주무시다, 계시다, 말씀하시다.
Where are you going? (to an elder)
드시다 replaces 먹다 in honorific speech.
To an elder: 'Where are you going?' =
Elder is the subject → 가 + 세요. Plain 가요 lacks the honorific.
The honorific verb for 먹다 / 마시다:
For a person being somewhere, 있다 becomes 계시다 → 계세요.
성함 is the honorific word for 이름.
A respected person being somewhere → 계세요.
When did you arrive? (to an elder)
Eating, for an elder, is 드시다 → 드세요.
To an elder: 'Where are you going?'
가 + 세요: the elder is the one going.
No 시 about yourself, and destination takes 에.
좀, 혹시, -아/어 주시겠어요?, -(으)면 안 돼요? — the softeners that get a yes.
By any chance, do you have an English menu?
Could you move us to a window seat?
Most polite way to ask someone to take a photo:
좀 slips in after the noun and softens the request.
'By any chance, do you have an English menu?' =
혹시 opens the question; 있어요? = do you have?
Asking a stranger: 'Would you mind taking a photo (for us)?' =
-아/어 주시겠어요 asks them to do it; -아/어도 돼요 asks if you may.
Politely refusing: 'Sorry, but that's not possible' =
안 돼요 = not possible. It's spelled 돼요, never 되요.
앉 + 아도 돼요 = may I sit.
Would it be okay if I sit here?
Would you mind taking a photo (for us)?
찍어 + 주시겠어요 = would you take (it) for me.
By any chance, is there a bathroom?
혹시 = by any chance; it opens the question.
May I take a photo? (use -아/어도 돼요)
Would it be okay if I sit here? (use -(으)면 안 돼요)
Consonant stem 앉 + 으면 안 돼요. This 안 is part of the set phrase, not a plain 'not'.
Titles, the 수고 family, email openers and closers, and surviving 회식.
Keep up the good work (to someone still working, as you leave)
Good work today (to a senior, after work)
Good work (to a junior or peer)
Hello, this is Kii from the marketing team
Please have a drink (pouring for a senior)
I have to drive, so (no thanks)
You're leaving; a coworker at your level is still working. You say:
수고하세요 = keep up the good work (they stay).
Address a manager named 김민수 as:
Politely declining a drink at 회식:
Give a reason; 운전 is the universal one.
Leaving while a coworker is still working, you say:
수고하세요 = keep up the good work, to someone who stays.
To your manager at the end of the day:
수고했어요 is for juniors or peers; seniors get 수고하셨습니다.
How do you address your manager (과장)?
The standard email closer 'Please take a look':
드림 goes after your own name; never 씨 or 님 for yourself.
I'll head out first (to the room)
먼저 퇴근하겠습니다 is the set phrase.
몇 시예요? = what time is it?
Hello, this is Kii from the marketing team
Team, then your name + 입니다. No 님 for yourself.
Good work today (to a senior, after work)
Seniors get the honorific past: 수고하셨습니다.
To your team lead after work: 'Good work today'
Title + 님, then the senior form 수고하셨습니다.
Leaving before your boss: 'I'll head out first'
Say it clearly to the room.
Manager, could you check this? (very polite)
Title + 님, then -아/어 주시겠어요 from the requests lesson.
